vignette:
Dr. Nguyễn sits perfectly still in the armchair, his back straight, hands resting flat on his knees. At seventy-seven, he still carries the disciplined posture of a surgeon—economy of motion, vigilance in stillness. He was the Chief of Surgery at a major metropolitan hospital for decades, renowned for hands that never trembled. His wife, Linh, brought him here. She started hiding the remote control because his startle response has grown so violent that he drops whatever he is holding at the sound of a helicopter on the evening news.

He tells his story as if presenting a case study. Dry. Precise. Without emotion.

“I was a resident in 1968. Saigon. The Tet Offensive.”

He was twenty-two years old. The hospital lost power. He operated by the light of a kerosene lamp for three days without sleep, sewing up soldiers and civilians, watching people die on the concrete floor because there was nowhere to put them. The trauma he witnessed was not his own injury—he was never shot—but the complete unraveling of every rule he believed governed the world.

He describes the moment that fractured him. He was coming down the stairs to grab more saline. He saw his professor, Dr. Phạm, being dragged into the hospital courtyard by a soldier. The professor was a thin, gray-haired man who liked to quote Camus. The soldier shot him in the back of the head. Dr. Nguyễn watched. He did not move. He could not make a sound. He stood there holding the saline bag, watching his teacher fall onto the red dirt. He never spoke of this to anyone for forty years.

“I worked,” he tells me quietly. “I operated. I came to America. I passed my boards. I had a family.”

The operating room became his sanctuary. The sterile field was a world he could control. If a bleeder popped, he could clamp it. If a patient was crashing, he could cut deeper to find the source. He was a god of order inside that room. The world outside—the memories, the refugee camps, the faces of the people he had to leave behind—was chaos he refused to touch.

He retired five years ago. The walls came down.

Last week, Linh was making bún bò Huế in the kitchen. The steam filled the house. The particular scent of lemongrass and fermented fish sauce hit him, and he was no longer in his suburban American kitchen. He was back in the hallway of that hospital in 1968. The smell of blood, monsoon rain, and cheap kerosene mixed with the broth. He dropped to his knees. He could not speak. He dissociated for what felt like hours. He saw Dr. Phạm’s face, clear as day, just before the bullet. He saw the look of quiet acceptance in the old man’s eyes.

“I was a witness,” he whispers. His hands are shaking for the first time in our session. “I did not stop it. I just stood there. I have been standing there for fifty-seven years.”

He now sleeps in a recliner in the living room, facing the front door. He checks the locks twelve times before bed. He canceled a trip to a surgical conference in Hanoi because the thought of the airplane engine makes his heart pound out of his chest. He refuses to go to the local Vietnamese grocery store. He avoids the community center. He avoids his own history.

He describes a profound numbness. He looks at his wife of fifty years and feels a thick pane of glass between them. His grandchildren call him the grumpy grandfather. He cannot feel joy. He feels only a constant, low-level irritability and a crushing guilt that he did nothing to save the man who taught him everything.

“I saved hundreds of lives,” he says, looking at the floor. “But I cannot stop seeing the one life I failed to save by just standing there and watching.”

He is a man who built a brilliant life on a foundation of deep, unspoken horror. The structure held for five decades. Now, the walls are groaning. The floor is giving way. He sits in my office, a titan of medicine, utterly powerless against the memory of a single moment he simply witnessed.
